title: Immunity: how a white blood cell decides what is a threat
method: Follow the mechanism: two candidates, one receptor match, one response
adaptation: A mechanism demonstration. A neutrophil meets a bacterium and a self cell at the same time; only the PAMP match triggers signalling, engulfment and cytokine recruitment.
question: How does a white blood cell know what to attack?
goal: Separate recognition (receptor–PAMP match) from response (signal cascade, phagocytosis, cytokines), and see why self markers do not trigger it.
assumptions: Schematic illustration: receptor shapes and PAMP spikes are simplified, the cell is not to scale, and the cytokine response is compressed. It shows the logic of innate recognition, not a molecular simulation.

quiz.prompt: What actually commits the neutrophil to attack?
quiz.explanation: Contact alone is not enough. The self cell is touched in passing and ignored; the decision is a receptor–PAMP match, which starts the signal cascade.

beats.title: A neutrophil on patrol
beats.question: What does the cell check before it attacks?
beats.narration: A neutrophil patrols with receptors on its surface. Before it commits, it has to test what it has touched.
beats.visual_change: The cell appears with a breathing halo and Y-shaped receptors probing outward.
beats.insight: Recognition happens at the membrane, before any response.

beats.title: Two candidates arrive
beats.question: Which of these should the cell attack?
beats.narration: A bacterium carrying PAMP spikes and a self cell carrying MHC-I markers arrive together. One is a threat; one is the body's own tissue.
beats.visual_change: Both objects approach; labels follow them, and the self cell passes without binding.
beats.insight: The cell must distinguish danger from self, not merely detect contact.

beats.title: Recognition is a molecular match
beats.question: What makes the bacterium different?
beats.narration: The receptor reaches the bacterial PAMP and locks on. That shape match is the recognition event. The self cell's markers never fit.
beats.visual_change: One receptor shifts into contact, “PAMP match” appears, and a flash marks the binding.
beats.insight: A receptor–PAMP match is the decision point.

beats.title: The signal reaches the nucleus
beats.question: How does a surface event change the cell's behaviour?
beats.narration: Binding sends a signal inward. Pulses travel to the nucleus, which brightens: the cell is now activated.
beats.visual_change: Three pulses travel along a path from the receptor to the nucleus; the nucleus changes colour.
beats.insight: Recognition is converted into an internal state change.

beats.title: Engulfment and digestion
beats.question: What does activation actually do?
beats.narration: Pseudopodia wrap around the bacterium and pull it inside. A phagosome forms, an oxidative burst follows, and the bacterium is digested.
beats.visual_change: Two membrane arcs close around the bacterium; it moves inside, a vesicle forms and the bacterium disappears.
beats.insight: The response is physical: the threat is internalised and destroyed.

beats.title: Call for help
beats.question: How does one cell turn into a response?
beats.narration: Cytokines leave the cell and recruit more neutrophils to the site.
beats.visual_change: Cytokine dots travel outward and two helper cells appear at the edges.
beats.insight: A local decision scales into a tissue-level response.

beats.title: The rule
beats.question: What should we remember?
beats.narration: PAMP match, attack. Self marker, ignore. That contrast is the whole logic of innate recognition.
beats.visual_change: The conclusion line appears and the neutrophil is highlighted.
beats.insight: Recognition specificity, not contact, determines the response.
